You talk about memories: ricordare and ricordarsi di, dimenticare and dimenticarsi di, mi viene / mi torna in mente, mi manca, rimpiangere, avere nostalgia di and the imperfetto for past habits (da piccola andavo…, solevo…).
to suddenly remember, to come back to mind
to be in the habit of (literary)
A song came back to me.
I miss the sea in Malta.
When I was little I always went to the market with Grandma.
To use ricordare (transitive) and ricordarsi di (reflexive): ricordo la casa / mi ricordo della casa.
To use ricordarsi / dimenticarsi di + infinitive: mi sono dimenticata di chiamarti.
To use venire in mente and tornare in mente, with the right agreement.
To use mancare, which works like piacere: mi manca il mare, mi mancate voi.
To distinguish rimpiangere and avere nostalgia di.
To use the imperfetto for past habits and recognise the literary verb solere.
Florence, late September. After six months in Malta, Giulia, Matei and Viola come back to Via Maggio. Viola is three years and four months old. Graziella is waiting for her at the trattoria door.
Viola! My little doll! Do you remember me?
Give her a moment, Grandma. She's tired from the journey.
She's looking at me like a stranger. She's forgotten me.
She hasn't forgotten. It's just that six months, at three, is a whole lifetime.
I know. But I missed her every single day. I missed the sound of her footsteps on the ceiling.
She thought about you too. Every evening in Malta she asked about "the soup grandma".
Look. She's sniffing the air. Something's coming back to her.
It's the soffritto. I was making it when you arrived.
There. She remembers the smell. Children remember smells before faces.
She said ribollita! She remembers! I'll never forget this moment.
"ti ricordi di me?" = do you remember me?
"le sta tornando in mente" = it's coming back to her
"non me lo dimenticherò" = I'll never forget it
Ricordo la casa di via Maggio.
I remember the house in Via Maggio.
Mi ricordo della casa di via Maggio.
Both versions are correct for "to remember something". For "not to forget to do something" use ricordarsi di + infinitive.
In the passato prossimo: ho dimenticato (with avere), but mi sono dimenticato / dimenticata (with essere, the participle agrees).
3. Venire in mente, tornare in mente
The thing remembered is the subject, and the person is in the dative (mi, ti, le…). In the passato prossimo essere is used:
Mi è venuta in mente una canzone.
Le sono tornati in mente i giorni di Malta.
The days in Malta came back to her.
The participle agrees with the thing remembered: venutA (una canzone), tornatI (i giorni).
"Mancare" works like "piacere": the thing missing is the subject. "Mi manchi" = you are missed by me, I miss you. Don't confuse it with "Io manco a te" (you miss me).
Da piccola andavo al mercato con la nonna.
Ernesto soleva lavorare fino a tardi.
"Solere" appears mostly in books and in the imperfetto (solevo, soleva). In speech you say "di solito" or "ero solito".
"Ernesto soleva lavorare fino a tardi" means:
Da dove tornano Giulia, Matei e Viola?
Pensa che Viola si sia dimenticata di lei
Il rumore dei passi di Viola sul soffitto
Come chiamava Viola Graziella a Malta?
Di che cosa si ricordano prima i bambini, secondo Giulia?
Le tacche e la ninna nanna

The Beheading restoration finished on 15 September, two weeks early, thanks to Karl, to the scaffolding that had never fallen and to Aldo's blue brush, which Graziella had brought to Malta in person in July, hidden in a flask labelled "herbal tea". The painting was presented to the public on a warm evening, before the Grand Master of the Order, the President of Malta and three hundred people who couldn't all fit into the oratory. The little T under the signature had not been touched. Next to the painting, on a panel, was the copy of the 1608 hospital register, with the line about Agata and Salvatore.

On the day of departure, Lina cried more than anyone. Viola gave her the cloth bunny "on loan", as she put it in her small serious voice, and Lina promised to bring it back to Florence at Christmas. Sister Agata gave Viola a painted wooden egg, "so you remember the hens". Camilleri and Marija took them to the airport, and before security Camilleri shook Giulia's hand for a long time. "Remember," he said, "that there's a house with a green gallarija here. For when you have another painting that looks at you." Giulia replied that she would never forget it.

All of Via Maggio was waiting for them in Florence. Not just the family: the baker, the fruit seller, the barman, Lorenzo, Rita, Signor Franco with his paddle, the prior of the confraternity with a tray of cantucci. Someone had hung a banner between two windows, handwritten by Davide: "Welcome back. We missed you." But Viola, getting out of the car, clung to Giulia's leg and looked at all those people with frightened eyes. Six months, at three, is half a memory. She didn't recognise anyone. Not even Graziella, who had put on her best apron for the occasion.

Graziella tried not to show it, but everyone noticed her lips were trembling. "Do you remember me, little doll?" she asked, bending down. Viola hid her face in her mother's trousers. There was an awkward silence. It was Matei who saved the situation, noticing that Viola was sniffing the air. From the trattoria door came the smell of soffritto, onion, celery and carrot in oil, which Graziella had left on the stove. Viola raised her head. She looked at the door. Then she looked at Graziella, and something passed through her eyes, like a light switching on in a dark room.

"Ribollita," she said. She didn't say it to anyone in particular. She said it the way you say a magic word, a password that opens a door. Graziella put a hand over her mouth. Then Viola let go of Giulia's leg, took three uncertain steps towards her and took hold of her apron with her little hand, as she used to before leaving, when she followed her into the kitchen. "Soup grandma," she said. Graziella picked her up and hugged her so tightly that Viola protested. Behind them, Signor Franco blew his nose into his signal paddle.

That evening at dinner Chiara gave her report on the six months at the workshop, with a notebook full of notes she had prepared "so as not to forget anything". She remembered everything: the three restorations finished, the silk altar cloth embroidered with Doina, the difficult client who wanted a Botticelli in three days, the times Davide had knocked over a jar of varnish and cleaned it all up before she noticed. "I noticed anyway," said Chiara, looking at Davide, who went red. "But I never told you. I'm telling you now." Bellini, from his corner, added that he had done the same thing in 1979 with a jar of rabbit-skin glue, and that his grandfather had found out thirty years later, reading an old diary. Everyone laughed. But Giulia noticed that Chiara didn't need the notebook: she knew it all by heart, day by day, the way you remember things done in fear and finished with pride.

But Viola's memory came back in pieces, like a mosaic put back together one tile at a time. That evening she remembered the stairs to the first floor, and climbed them on her own, counting the steps in Italian and Maltese. The next day she remembered Lupino, who had been waiting for her under the table for six months and who, when he saw her, started running in circles around the trattoria barking like mad. On the third day she remembered the Santo Spirito market, and asked the fruit seller for strawberries, which weren't available in September. But some things she didn't remember at all. Her little room, for example.

Pietro had looked after the little room, as he had promised in March. He had kept it tidy, dusted the toys every week, even watered the little plant on the windowsill. But when Viola went in, she looked at it the way you look at another little girl's room. She sat on the bed, touched the blankets, looked out of the window. Then she asked, in Italian with a slightly Maltese accent: "Where's the sea?" Pietro, who had waited six months for that moment, felt his heart sink. He went down to the kitchen and told his grandmother quietly: "She doesn't remember her room. She misses Malta."

Graziella didn't answer straight away. She finished stirring the sauce, wiped her hands on her apron, and went up to the little room with Pietro. Viola was still sitting on the bed, looking at the rooftops of Florence as if they were the sea at Valletta. Graziella sat down next to her without a word. Then, softly, she began to sing. Not a Florentine song. She sang Viorica's lullaby, the one Doina had taught her word by word in March, in a Romanian full of Tuscan accent that would have made anyone laugh. But Viola didn't laugh.

At the second verse Viola turned round. At the third she rested her head on Graziella's arm. By the end of the song she was humming along too, in Romanian, in Maltese and in a language all her own. Then she looked up at the door and her eyes stopped on the door frame, where the family's notches were. She got up and went to touch them with her finger, one by one, from the bottom up, as Pietro did. She stopped at hers, the one from when she was two, with her name written in pencil. She looked at it for a long time. "Viola," she read, even though she couldn't read. "It's mine."

Pietro ran to get the pencil. Marco came up the stairs with the tape measure. Giulia and Matei came from the kitchen. And so, on the evening of their return, with the whole family squeezed into the little room, Viola got her new notch, three years and four months, eight centimetres higher than the March one. "She grew in Malta," said Graziella, with a hint of jealousy. "The sea makes you grow," replied Matei. "Yes," said Graziella, "but ribollita makes you remember." And from that moment Viola stopped asking about the sea.

The next day Matei went to the workshop with a cloth handkerchief in his hand. Inside was Ernesto's small brush, clean, as Bellini had asked in March. Bellini took it, held it up to the light, checked the bristles one by one with a magnifying glass. Then he nodded. "It has touched Saint John," he said. "You can see it." "How can you see it?" asked Matei. Bellini smiled. "You can't," he admitted. "But I remember, because I gave it to you. And at a certain age, memories are worth more than eyes." He put the brush back in its case, next to Ernesto's others, and locked the drawer.

In the following days Pietro invented a game to help Viola remember. He called it "Do you remember?". Every evening before dinner he showed her something from the house or the neighbourhood and asked if she remembered it: the ginger cat at the newspaper office, the workshop bell, Signor Franco's paddle, the tin box with Aldo's letters. If Viola said yes, she earned an extra spoonful of ribollita. If she said no, Pietro told her a story about that thing, and the next day asked her again. After two weeks Viola remembered everything, even things she had never seen, like Grandpa's red bicycle in 1966. "That's not remembering," Giulia protested, laughing. "That's making things up." Pietro shook his head, very seriously. "It's the same thing," he replied. "The professor taught me. A memory told well becomes true."

Then Matei went to Sibiu for a weekend, to take his father back his silver pocket watch. Ion was waiting for him at the station, as always, ten minutes early. Matei put it in his hand without a word. Ion opened it, looked at the dial, compared it with the station clock. "Still exact," he said. "I knew it." Then he closed it and put it back in his pocket, in the waistcoat pocket where it had been for forty years. "Do you remember," he asked Matei, "when you were little and I took you to the station on Sundays to watch the trains?" Matei smiled. "I remember every time I take a train," he replied.

That evening, in the house in Sibiu, Doina brought out a cardboard box Matei had never seen. Inside were photographs from the theatre: embroidered costumes, made-up actors, a young woman with pins between her lips adjusting the hem of a queen's dress. "That's me," said Doina. "In 1979. I was twenty-two." Then she brought out another photo, older, of an elderly woman with a headscarf and light eyes. "And this is Viorica," she said. "My mother. Do you remember her?" Matei looked at it for a long time. He was five when she died. He didn't remember her face. But he remembered the song.

"She used to sing it to me in the evening," Matei said softly. "Sitting on my bed, with her hands in her lap. I remember she had rough hands and smelled of bread." Doina nodded, her eyes wet. "She baked bread every morning at five," she said. "For forty years. You remember the smell because it's the last thing you forget." Matei thought of Viola at the trattoria door, sniffing the soffritto before recognising her grandmother. He thought of Graziella and the loaf of 1966. And he understood that, in that family, memory always passed through the kitchen.

Doina gave him the photo of Viorica. "Take it to Florence," she said. "Put it next to Aldo's, in the trattoria kitchen. So that when the little one is grown up and no longer remembers anything of these years, she'll see the faces of those who left her the songs and the recipes." Matei put it in his wallet, next to the photo of Viola on the green gallarija. On the train home, watching the Romanian countryside rush past the window, he realised he didn't miss anything. Not Malta, not Sibiu, not Florence. He had them all in his memory.

So, one Sunday in October, on the shelf in the trattoria kitchen, next to the tin box with the thirteen letters, the blue brush and the photo of Aldo with the red bicycle, a new photograph appeared: an elderly woman with a headscarf and light eyes, smiling in front of a stone oven. Graziella looked at it for a long time. Then she put a small glass of wine in front of it, as they do in villages for the dead who are remembered with affection. "Welcome, Viorica," she said. "Here we sing your song every evening. Even if with the wrong accent."

Viola, who was passing by with Lupino, stopped in front of the shelf and looked at the two photographs, Aldo and Viorica, side by side. She asked who they were. Graziella explained in simple words: the grandpa with the bicycle and the grandma with the song. Viola thought about it with the seriousness of a three-year-old. Then she pointed at Aldo and said "ribollita", pointed at Viorica and said "nanna". Graziella laughed. "Exactly," she said. "You've understood everything. One makes you eat, the other makes you sleep. And both of them make you remember."

That night, before going to sleep, Pietro wrote in the notebook where he copied his grandfather's sentences a sentence of his own, the first he really felt he had written by himself: "Memory is like the door frame of the little room. The notches don't get erased, even when you forget you made them. All it takes is a smell, or a song, and you find them all again, one above the other, from the bottom up." He read it again, found it a bit too poetic, and thought of crossing it out. Then he remembered Bellini, who always said that your first true sentences should not be corrected. And he left it as it was.

The following Saturday, at the open workshop, a German tourist asked Pietro, who was acting as guide, what the tin box was that could be seen in an old photo on the wall, next to Davide's drawing. Pietro was about to answer with the explanation he always gave, the short and precise one. Then he stopped. His grandfather came back to mind, the attic, the twelve letters never sent. And instead of the short explanation, he sat down on the workshop step and told the whole story, from the beginning, in the passato remoto. The tourist listened for half an hour without interrupting. At the end he said only, in uncertain Italian: "Thank you. I won't forget it."
